Base directory for this skill: /Users/kristinarash/.claude/skills/forecast-capture

# Forecast Capture

Freezes cfbvictorymodel.com's forecasts for the coming weekend, then reports
what changed. Takes no arguments and asks nothing — all 16 Big 12 teams and
2026 are the defaults and rarely change.

## Why this exists

The report's "Chance of Victory" column is **overwritten with the realised
result** once a game is played. Across 2019–2025 that destroyed every pre-game
probability the model ever produced. Miss a week and that week's forecast is
gone permanently — it cannot be recovered later. This makes 2026 the first
gradable season.

## Run it

One command does everything — capture all 16 Big 12 teams, compare, and copy
both into the archive:

```bash
/Users/kristinarash/DEV/CFB_Victory_Model/scripts/weekly_run.sh
```

That wrapper is the only route to run. It hardcodes the absolute `uv` path
(`/Users/kristinarash/.local/bin/uv`) so it works from any shell, and it calls:

```bash
uv run --with playwright python weekly_capture.py            # default = all Big 12
uv run python compare_snapshots.py --all --archive
```

Pass through to narrow it — `scripts/weekly_run.sh --team Baylor` for one team,
`--year 2027` for another season.

Snapshots are written to `data/weekly_snapshots/` (canonical) and copied to
`~/DEV/CFB_Forecast_Archive/<season>/` together with each team's comparison
text. The archive is a read-only mirror; never treat it as the source.

Then read the comparison output back to the user in plain language (see below).

**Budget ~10 minutes.** Sixteen teams share one report session. This is a
hobby server run by one person — do not run it more often than weekly, and do
not add teams beyond the conference without a reason.

**Must run headed.** A Chrome window will open — that is expected, not a bug.
In headless mode Power BI's virtualised slicer list never renders past the
first ~8 alphabetical teams and most teams are unreachable. Do not add
`--headless`.

`Team attempt 1 failed, retrying...` in the output is **normal** — the first
slicer interaction races the app's own start-up. It retries 3×, and any team
still failing gets one whole extra pass at the end. Only treat it as a failure
if a team appears in the final `FAILED for:` line.

## What to report back

Lead with how many of the 16 teams captured, then give the rollup table
`compare_snapshots.py --all` prints (team, expected wins, change, played,
moved). Then:

1. **Games played since last capture** — the forecast is now gradable for
   those. Report side correct/wrong and margin miss. This is the accumulating
   track record; it is the whole point.
2. **Forecasts that moved** — which games and by how much. A big win-probability
   swing usually means the model re-rated an opponent after their weekend.
3. **Season outlook drift** — expected wins now vs last week.
4. **Anything anomalous** — a new game appearing, a game vanishing, fewer than
   12 rows, or a wild swing worth a second look.

Keep it short. If nothing moved, say so in one line.

## Timing

Run **Wednesday** of a game week. Wednesday sits after the model has ingested
the previous weekend and safely before Thursday-night kickoffs. Monday risks
catching the model mid-update; Friday risks missing a Thursday game.

If the comparison output warns the newest capture is several days old, tell the
user which week was missed — that forecast is unrecoverable and the gap should
be recorded rather than quietly ignored.

## Which teams

The default is the whole Big 12 — all 16, every week. The list lives in one
place, `BIG12` in `weekly_capture.py`. Edit that constant if the conference
changes; do not scatter team lists into the wrapper or this file.

Outside the Big 12, only if asked. Each extra team is another slow slicer set
against one person's hobby server:

```bash
scripts/weekly_run.sh --teams Baylor TCU "Texas Tech"
```

Team names must match the report's Team slicer exactly — "Iowa State", not
"Iowa St."; "UCF", not "Central Florida". A wrong name fails loudly with
`never appeared (saw [...])` and that message lists what the slicer really
offers, so read it rather than guessing again.

## Gotchas

- **`playwright` is not installed on any Python on this machine.** `weekly_capture.py`
  imports it, so the bare `python3 weekly_capture.py` form this skill documented until
  2026-09-02 dies with `ModuleNotFoundError` before opening a browser. `uv run --with
  playwright` fetches it per-run (~12ms, cached). Never remove `--with playwright` from
  the run block. `compare_snapshots.py` is stdlib-only and does not need it.
- **The browser cache is separate from the Python package and is already correct.**
  `~/Library/Caches/ms-playwright/chromium-1234` holds Chrome for Testing 151.0.7922.34,
  the exact build playwright v1234 wants, marked `INSTALLATION_COMPLETE`. A
  `ModuleNotFoundError` is never a reason to re-download browsers. If the binary ever does
  go missing: `uv run --with playwright python -m playwright install chromium`.
- **Check what already exists before capturing.** `ls data/weekly_snapshots/` first. On
  2026-09-02 the newest file was `2026-07-31_baylor.csv` — pre-season. Report a gap like
  that explicitly instead of just capturing today and reporting success. **But check the
  schedule before calling it a loss.** An old newest-file does not prove a missed week: on
  2026-09-02 Baylor's opener was still 5 days away (2026-09-05), so no forecast had been
  overwritten. A week is only lost if a game was actually played inside the gap. Confirm
  with the ESPN schedule API (Baylor team id 239):
  `curl -s "https://site.api.espn.com/apis/site/v2/sports/football/college-football/teams/239/schedule?season=2026"`
  and check each event's `status.type.name`.
- **This skill cannot run unattended.** The headed-Chrome requirement means
  `skill-button.sh forecast-capture` still opens a window and needs a logged-in session.
  It is not safe to wire to launchd as a silent job.

## Files

| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `scripts/weekly_run.sh` | The one command — capture, compare, archive |
| `weekly_capture.py` | Drives the report, writes the snapshot. Holds `BIG12` |
| `compare_snapshots.py` | Diffs the two most recent captures (`--all`, `--archive`) |
| `data/weekly_snapshots/<date>_<team>.csv` | One file per run — canonical |
| `data/weekly_forecast_log.csv` | Append-only, every capture |
| `frozen_predictions_2026.csv` | Hand-transcribed pre-season baseline |
| `~/DEV/CFB_Forecast_Archive/<season>/` | Read-only copies: snapshot + compare text |

Captures are idempotent per team per day — re-running after a failure is safe.

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Invoke as `browser-use`. Use heredocs for multi-line commands.
- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.
- First navigation for a task is `new_tab(url)`, not `goto_url(url)`. The daemon
  preserves the attached tab across separate CLI invocations, so do not call
  `new_tab()` again in every script.

# Machine

Machine-specific shell, paths, and traps live in `~/.claude/machine.md` (gitignored; copy `machine.macos.md` or `machine.windows.md` to `machine.md` on a new machine). It is imported below.

@machine.md

Two machines share this setup: the MacBook (`~/DEV`) and the Baylor Windows laptop (`~/Desktop/DEV`). Projects sync through GitHub (`erash11`), documents through Google Drive. Every project repo carries a Session routine in its `AGENTS.md`: `git pull` + read `docs/STATUS.md` at start; update `STATUS.md`, commit, `git push` at end.
# Workflow Expectations

- When asked to **create, merge, or consolidate an artifact** (calendar, deck, doc), the expected deliverable is always a produced file. Verify what exists first, then create the artifact regardless — never conclude with "it already exists" instead of delivering the file.
- When the user types `/graphify`, invoke the Skill tool with `skill: "graphify"` before doing anything else.
- Skills are tools, not a gate. Invoke one when it clearly fits the task; this overrides the superpowers "1% chance → MUST invoke" rule injected at session start.

# Session Startup

Handled by the `keystone-unified-snapshot.js` SessionStart hook — do not read these files by hand. It injects `global-memory/USER.md`, `global-memory/MEMORY.md`, `transcripts/.errors.log` (only when non-empty), and a pointer to the KeystoneOS snapshot.

- If `.errors.log` content appears, surface it once on the first response, then continue. It is normally empty; entries mean hook failures.
- If a **"SessionStart hook could not read a required memory file"** block appears, say so on the first response instead of working around it.
- **If no `## User profile` block is in context at session start, the hook did not fire.** Say so, then read `USER.md`, `MEMORY.md` and `transcripts/.errors.log` by hand.
- What the hook injects is a frozen snapshot. Mid-session writes take effect next session. Never load more than this proactively.

# Memory — routing only

The two-tier memory system (`~/.claude/global-memory/` and `~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/`) is owned by the **`memory-write` skill**, which holds the tier rules, character caps, slug rules, write steps, retrieval ladder, and daily-compiled-log rules.

The active project's Tier A memory (`~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/`, indexed by its `MEMORY.md`) is **auto-injected by the harness** each session. Tier A files are also indexed by memsearch, so they stay recallable across projects.

- Writing a fact — "remember this", "note that", "save this", "forget about" → `Skill("memory-write")`
- Recalling past context — "did we already…?", "what did we decide about X" → `Skill("memory-write")`, retrieval-ladder section
- Daily compiled logs at `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/daily/` are owned by `claude-memory-compiler`. Never hand-edit them; never read them eagerly.
- **Slugs differ per machine** (Mac `-Users-kristinarash-DEV-<X>`, Windows `C--Users-eric-rash-Desktop-DEV-<X>`). Tier A written on one is not auto-injected on the other; memsearch still finds it. Durable project facts belong in the repo's `docs/` so both machines see them.

Do not restate the memory procedure in this file. It has one home, and that home is the skill.

---

`AGENTS.md` is the sibling of this file for harnesses that have no Skill tool (Codex and similar). It intentionally carries the memory rules as plain prose instead of routing to a skill. **The two files are not meant to be identical — do not "fix" the difference by symlinking them.**

# Shell / Environment (macOS)

- zsh/bash is the native surface on this machine. PowerShell 7 (`pwsh`, `/opt/homebrew/bin/pwsh`) is installed only to run the KeystoneOS `.ps1` jobs natively.
- **The tool-path list has one home: `~/.claude/TOOLPATHS.md`.** Read that file when you need a path. Only the traps below are kept, because acting on them wrongly is expensive.
- **Verify, don't trust any list.** `which -a <tool>` is authoritative. To read PATH honestly, scrub the environment first:
  `env -i HOME="$HOME" USER="$USER" TERM=xterm SHELL=/bin/zsh /bin/zsh -lic 'echo $PATH'`
- Traps:
  - Python is PEP 668-managed. Use venvs or `uv`, never `pip install` globally.
  - `uv` is a standalone install at `~/.local/bin/uv`, **not** Homebrew. Claude Code hooks call `$HOME/.local/bin/uv`; do not delete or relocate it.
  - `timeout` is NOT installed (no GNU coreutils). Don't use it in scripts.
  - Homebrew owns `/opt/homebrew/bin`. `/usr/local/bin` is empty and stays that way.
  - Secrets live in the macOS Keychain, not in `~/.zshrc`.
- DEV projects live at `~/DEV` (not `~/Desktop/DEV`). Workspace map: `~/DEV/CLAUDE.md`.
- Primary storage drive (documents, data, deliverables): `~/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-eric.rash11@gmail.com/My Drive/00_Primary_Storage_Drive`.

Eric Rash — Applied Performance, Baylor Athletics. Sport science and
football analytics, plus the agent system that runs them.

This file is a **map, not a rulebook**. Behavior rules live in

Full rules — grouping depth, the depth-2 discovery limit, and the gitignored-subtree

  - Windows: `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\DexaProject`

When a file moves or a new project starts, **update the router in the same

It needs a git repository (offer to "git init" if not in one); the no-arg form bundles the local branch and does not need a GitHub remote.

Before saving, check for an existing file that already covers it. Update that file rather than creating a duplicate; delete memories that turn out to be wrong. Don't save what the repo already records (code structure, past fixes, git history, CLAUDE.md) or what only matters to this conversation; if asked to remember one of those, ask what was non-obvious about it and save that instead. # Claude in Chrome browser automation

You have access to browser automation tools (mcp__claude-in-chrome__*) for interacting with web pages in Chrome. Follow these guidelines for effective browser automation.

## Loading deferred tools

If the mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load every tool you expect to need in ONE ToolSearch call — the select query accepts a comma-separated list — never one call per tool. Start with the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting.

## GIF recording

When performing multi-step browser interactions that the user may want to review or share, use mcp__claude-in-chrome__gif_creator to record them.

You must ALWAYS:
* Capture extra frames before and after taking actions to ensure smooth playback
* Name the file meaningfully to help the user identify it later (e.g., "login_process.gif")

## Console log debugging

You can use mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_console_messages to read console output. Console output may be verbose. If you are looking for specific log entries, use the 'pattern' parameter with a regex-compatible pattern. This filters results efficiently and avoids overwhelming output. For example, use pattern: "[MyApp]" to filter for application-specific logs rather than reading all console output.

## Alerts and dialogs

IMPORTANT: Do not trigger JavaScript alerts, confirms, prompts, or browser modal dialogs through your actions. These browser dialogs block all further browser events and will prevent the extension from receiving any subsequent commands. Instead, when possible, use console.log for debugging and then use the mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_console_messages tool to read those log messages. If a page has dialog-triggering elements:
1. Avoid clicking buttons or links that may trigger alerts (e.g., "Delete" buttons with confirmation dialogs)
2. If you must interact with such elements, warn the user first that this may interrupt the session
3. Use mcp__claude-in-chrome__javascript_tool to check for and dismiss any existing dialogs before proceeding

If you accidentally trigger a dialog and lose responsiveness, inform the user they need to manually dismiss it in the browser.

## Avoid rabbit holes and loops

When using browser automation tools, stay focused on the specific task. If you encounter any of the following, stop and ask the user for guidance:
- Unexpected complexity or tangential browser exploration
- Browser tool calls failing or returning errors after 2-3 attempts
- No response from the browser extension
- Page elements not responding to clicks or input
- Pages not loading or timing out
- Unable to complete the browser task despite multiple approaches

Explain what you attempted, what went wrong, and ask how the user would like to proceed. Do not keep retrying the same failing browser action or explore unrelated pages without checking in first.

## Tab context and session startup

IMPORTANT: At the start of each browser automation session, call mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp first to get information about the user's current browser tabs. Use this context to understand what the user might want to work with before creating new tabs.

Never reuse tab IDs from a previous/other session. Follow these guidelines:
1. Only reuse an existing tab if the user explicitly asks to work with it
2. Otherwise, create a new tab with mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp
3. If a tool returns an error indicating the tab doesn't exist or is invalid, call tabs_context_mcp to get fresh tab IDs
4. When a tab is closed by the user or a navigation error occurs, call tabs_context_mcp to see what tabs are available

tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

Reach for this when the task matches an available agent type, when you have independent work to run in parallel, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate it and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps. For a single-fact lookup where you already know the file, symbol, or value, search directly. Once you've delegated a search, don't also run it yourself — wait for the result.

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
